newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity's Pozen says already staunching exodus.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity's Pozen says already staunching exodus.

text.p: The new president of Fidelity Management and Research Co., investment adviser to America's largest family of mutual funds, said Monday he is working to stem the exodus of portfolio managers from the company -- after the latest executive left.
Robert Pozen made his remarks after Fidelity confirmed that Bart Grenier, 38, the assistant head of the privately held company's stock division and former research chief, was leaving.

Pozen, 50, was promoted from general counsel to president and chief executive officer of a company that manages $500 billion in assets. He replaces Gary Burkhead, who moves up to vice chairman of Fidelity's parent company, FMR Corp.

Pozen, who has been with Fidelity for 10 years, said he also had advised people in Washington that he was no longer interested in any government position. As recently as April 7, he had been rumoured to be the next deputy U.S. Trade Representative in charge of Asia.
About 25 portfolio managers, including Magellan Fund chief Jeffrey Vinik, have left for competitors.

"We've bit the bullet and made the tough decisions last year in the equity group," Pozen said in an interview. "We now have people well positioned. We've reviewed the comp(ensation) systems and what we're really going to do is keep the themes of continuity and stability.
"There will always be some defections. There's no way you can stop that," he said.

Pozen, a lawyer with no investing background, said, "Think about what this job is from a functional role ... this is a management job. It involves going down the organisation managing personnel, reviewing performance, designing appropriate comp(ensation) systems, providing technology support. These are all things that I've been very involved with at Fidelity before."
He said the job comes down to "being a good people manager and really knowing how to work the Fidelity organisation and make things happen. That's what these people need."

But Alpha Equity Research's David O'Leary, a Fidelity watcher, said Pozen's legal background "will increase the friction with the star portfolio (managers) and probably accelerate defections in the coming weeks."
"This change creates a wide gap between senior management and portfolio managers that could have a negative impact on Fidelity's future growth and performance," O'Leary said.
O'Leary said Fidelity funds as a group underperformed other mutual funds.

He said the Vanguard S&P 500 fund was up 86 percent over the last three years, but noted that Fidelity's Growth and Income Fund was up 75 percent, Fidelity's ContraFund was up 65 percent and Magellan, the nation's largest mutual fund, was up 55 percent for the same period.
